title: Backoff, jitter and retry budgets
subtitle: Retries rescue one request but can sink a whole system. Here is how to retry without making an outage worse.

c.v: On 12 June 2025, many Google Cloud APIs returned 503 errors around the world. A bad policy record made Service Control, the system that checks API requests, crash again and again.
Google's engineers found the cause within 10 minutes. Within 40 minutes, they had rolled out a switch that turned the failing code path off.
That should have been the end. But in large regions like us-central1, the restarting Service Control tasks all hit the Spanner table they depend on. Google calls this a "
The report says Service Control "did not have the appropriate randomized
implemented to avoid this." Engineers throttled task creation to protect that database. Full recovery in us-central1 took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes.
So the bug caused the outage, but the missing backoff stretched the recovery. One of Google's fixes: "audit and ensure our systems employ randomized exponential backoff."
need a key, a limit and backoff with
. This lesson is about the system as a whole. One retry helps one request. Millions of retries can keep a failing service down.
Brooker calls retries "selfish": "when a client retries, it spends more of the server's time to get a higher chance of success".
That is fine when failures are rare. It is dangerous when the server fails because it is overloaded.
Spread retries out in time (backoff with jitter), keep them in one layer, and give them a budget. When the budget runs out, fail fast instead of retrying.
You saw in the last lesson that retries multiply when several layers retry. Here are the numbers when each layer makes 1 try plus 3 retries. Step through it with Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Google's SRE book gives the same example: 3 layers that each make 4 attempts send 64 attempts to the database for one user action.
Brooker's example has five layers with 3 tries each: 3^5 = 243 times the database load.
The fix is to retry at one point in the stack. That is Amazon's best practice for low-cost operations.
Google adds a rule: only the layer just above the one that failed retries. If its retries fail, it returns an "overloaded; don't retry" error, so callers higher up do not retry again.
Amazon does not say which layer. Google picks the layer just above the failure. The diagram lets the app retry. Either way, only one layer retries.
Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure. Without a limit, the wait grows without end, so implementations set a maximum wait.
The AWS SDKs, for example, cap each backoff at 20 seconds.
Backoff alone is not enough. In Brooker's 2015 simulation, clients that failed together backed off together. They still arrived in clusters, so contention "hasn't been reduced much".
Jitter adds randomness to each wait. Here are the three rules from the simulator code behind the 2015 post, rewritten as small functions.

In the simulation, with 100 clients competing for the same resource, jitter cut the number of calls by more than half compared with plain backoff.
Full jitter did the least work. Decorrelated jitter finished slightly sooner but made more calls. Equal jitter was the weakest of the three.

Jitter helps outside retries too. Amazon considers adding jitter to "all timers, periodic jobs, and other delayed work".
Restarting tasks, like Google's, need it as well.
Backoff spreads retries out. It does not limit their total. When a backend is down for everyone, every request fails, and every request retries. You need a
Google uses two limits. Each request gets at most three attempts. Each client also retries only while retries stay below 10% of its requests.
Without the client budget, load can grow to just under 3 times. With it, load grows about 1.1 times.
The SRE book also gives a per-process example: 60 retries a minute, then fail instead of retrying.

c.v: Draw the call chain in design reviews. Ask:
"Which layer retries? How many attempts in total, top to bottom?"
Read your library's defaults. HTTP clients, SDKs,
and queues often retry on their own.
Ask what happens when the backend is down for everyone, not just for one request. A budget should cap the total.
Tell callers how to behave when you are overloaded: a 503 with
to say when to come back, or a "don't retry" error so upper layers do not retry.

Watch the retry rate on a dashboard. A rising retry rate is an early warning of overload.

q.v: The service calls the database, and the database rejects the call as overloaded. Under Google's rule, which layer retries?

options.v: Every layer, so each one gets another chance.
Only the service, the layer just above the database.
Only the app at the top, because it knows the user.

why.v: Google retries only at the layer just above the one that failed. If that fails, it returns "overloaded; don't retry" so no one higher retries.

q.v: With full jitter, how long does a client wait before retry number n?

options.v: Exactly base × 2^n, so every client waits the same time.
A random time between 0 and min(cap, base × 2^n).
Half of min(cap, base × 2^n), plus a small random part.

why.v: Full jitter picks the whole wait at random, up to the capped backoff. The third option is equal jitter.

q.v: A client sends 1,000 requests a second and keeps retries under 10% of its requests. The backend fails every call. About how many retries a second can the client send?

why.v: A 10% retry budget caps retries at about 100 a second, so total load stays near 1.1×.

q.v: Which response is worth retrying, after a wait?

options.v: 400 Bad Request, because a field is missing.
503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After of 30 seconds.
403 Forbidden, because the token has no access.

why.v: A 503 may pass, and Retry-After says how long to wait. The other two will fail the same way again.
